clue.text: Place for meeting? Get on with opportunity

parts.note: to get on a ship or train is to board it
room, as in room for improvement, is scope or opportunity

explanation.surface: Office-speak: a job candidate told to climb aboard and seize the moment.
explanation.definitionFit: The board of directors convenes in its own dedicated chamber, the meeting place of a company's governing body.

clue.text: Touch base at start (career meeting)

indicators.note: says the base letter goes at the front of the next piece

parts.note: B is a standard abbreviation for base
to career is to rush headlong

explanation.surface: Jargon of the office: touching base with a colleague at the start of a careers meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'meeting' is a link word joining the pieces; 'Touch' is the definition and 'base' is wordplay, despite the stock phrase 'touch base'.
explanation.definitionFit: A light passing contact is a brush, so the two words are synonyms as verbs of contact.

clue.text: Account right? Gross "on my radar", say

indicators.note: gross in the sense of disgusting or ugly signals the two little words being mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: A manager asking whether a gross figure is on their radar, in business jargon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gross' is read as revenue but is the anagram signal working on ON MY to give ONYM.
explanation.definitionFit: Radar was formed from initial letters of radio detection and ranging, so it is an example of such a word.

clue.text: Plan which might be taken on board, we hear

indicators.note: says the word meant is to be judged by how it sounds when spoken

parts.words: which might be taken on board
parts.note: a draught is a counter moved around a draughtboard (a checkers piece)

explanation.surface: A plan that colleagues might take on board, in meeting-room language.
explanation.walkthrough: Draughts is the British name for checkers, so a draught is a piece on its board; DRAUGHT and DRAFT are pronounced the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A draft is a preliminary version or outline, so it serves as a synonym for a plan.

clue.text: Contract beginning — beginners perform better in business

indicators.note: to contract a word is to shorten it, here by cutting its final letter

parts.note: the outset of something is its beginning
L stands for learner, so two beginners give two of that letter

explanation.surface: At the start of a contract, novices outperform the old hands commercially.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contract' looks like a business noun but is an instruction to drop the last letter of OUTSET, leaving OUTSE; L is the learner-driver plate letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To outsell rivals is to beat them in sales volume, a direct business sense of doing better.

clue.text: Lethal drink knocked back roused drunk

indicators.note: a drink knocked back is downed, and here it also means the word is read backwards

parts.note: rum is a spirit, so a drink

indicators.note: drunk signals the letters of roused being jumbled

explanation.surface: A drinker downs a glass and, roused and drunk, turns deadly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocked back' doubles as drinking slang and the reversal of RUM to MUR; 'drunk' turns ROUSED into DEROUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Something murderous is capable of killing, which is what deadly or fatal means.

clue.text: Member worried partner

parts.note: M is an abbreviation for member, as in MP
to worry at something is to gnaw it, so ate can mean worried, as in what ate him

explanation.surface: A club member fretting about their other half.
explanation.definitionFit: A mate is a friend, spouse or companion, all senses of the word for a close associate.

clue.text: Regularly in day they replace English with bull, ultimately

parts.note: Mon is the abbreviation for Monday

indicators.note: replace together with with tells us one letter is swapped out for another
pairs with replace, naming what goes in

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word bull

explanation.surface: Office talk of colleagues who daily swap plain English for bull, meaning jargon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bull' in the surface is jargon or nonsense; here 'ultimately' takes only its final letter as the replacement for the English letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Monthly as an adverb means at intervals of a month, a particular way of happening at regular times.

clue.text: Director managed to cut rubbish ("in loop")

indicators.note: one piece cuts into another, so it sits inside it

parts.note: tat is cheap, shoddy goods: rubbish
to have run a business is to have managed it
the letter O is loop-shaped

explanation.surface: Someone who managed to throw out the rubbish while being kept in the loop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to cut' looks like the purpose of managing, but it says one piece goes inside the other; 'in loop' is meeting-room jargon read literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Quentin Tarantino is the American film-maker behind Pulp Fiction, so an example of a director.

clue.text: This paper's ignoring another? Front of Times showing full face

indicators.note: ignoring means leaving that letter out of the word

parts.note: the puzzle appears in the Guardian, so this paper is the Guardian
the i is another British daily newspaper, giving the letter I

indicators.note: the front of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: The Guardian snubs a rival paper, while the Times front page shows a full-face portrait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'another' is a second paper, the i, so GUARDIAN loses an I to give GUARDAN.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry, a beast described as guardant has its head turned to face the viewer.

clue.text: Stopped spouting rubbish, primarily, with year in retirement

indicators.note: primarily means first, taking the opening letter of rubbish

parts.note: and joins things just as with does

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the word for year is turned round

explanation.surface: Someone who stopped talking nonsense once they reached retirement.
explanation.definitionFit: A source that ran dry stopped flowing, so the idiom means ceased gushing or spouting.

clue.text: IT system in hospital dividing opinion

indicators.note: dividing means splitting the other word by sitting within it

parts.note: a tenet is a held belief or opinion
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: A new computer system in a hospital that splits staff opinion.
explanation.definitionFit: The internet, often called just 'the net', is the global computer network, an information technology system.

clue.text: See 22 down
Got up to speed: final letter about low returns

indicators.note: about means going around, so the letter's name surrounds the other piece

parts.note: zed is the last letter of the alphabet

indicators.note: returns tells us the cow's word is read backwards

parts.note: to low is what cattle do, to moo

explanation.surface: Office talk: a final letter about poor returns has someone briefed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got up to speed' means accelerated here, not 'briefed'; ZED is the British name for the letter Z.
explanation.definitionFit: To zoom is to go very fast, so having zoomed is having reached a high speed.

clue.text: Working with those people? Stop improving

parts.note: a machine that is on is working
them refers to those people
to end is to stop

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether to keep collaborating with a certain group or call a halt.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone recovering from illness, getting better day by day.

clue.text: No good stopping awful "heads up" for business gatherings

indicators.note: stopping means plugging a gap, so these letters sit inside the others
awful signals the letters of the phrase being wrecked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A colleague's terrible heads-up being no help for corporate meetings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'business' is a euphemism for droppings, so the definition is heaps of dung, not conferences.
explanation.definitionFit: Animals do their business, so piles of manure are, cheekily, gatherings of that business.

clue.text: Throw in "on close of play" as filling — it's bedlam

indicators.note: as filling means placed inside like a sandwich filling

parts.note: to lob is to throw in a high arc
taken as written

indicators.note: the close of a word is its final letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cricket-like instruction to throw in at the close of play.
explanation.walkthrough: Bedlam, from London's old Bethlem hospital, can mean an asylum as well as chaos.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedlam was a name for a mental asylum, and the slang phrase means the same institution.

clue.text: It's reflected within uses for pay

indicators.note: within means placed inside the other word

parts.note: to spend money or time is to use it up

indicators.note: reflected means mirrored, so the two letters read the other way

parts.note: the 's is read as is, linking; the word it is the piece

explanation.surface: Someone reflecting on how a salary is used up.
explanation.definitionFit: A stipend is a fixed regular salary, especially for clergy, so a form of payment.

clue.text: Place for business? Proactive to work with rest

indicators.note: to work letters is to knead them into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A proactive boss wanting staff to work alongside everyone else.
explanation.definitionFit: The private sector is the part of the economy run by firms rather than the state, the realm of business.

clue.text: Hears director invested after section walks

indicators.note: after means the following piece comes after the section letter
invested means put inside, like money put into a venture

parts.note: a judge hears or tries a case

explanation.surface: A judge hears that a director has invested after a company division walks out.
explanation.definitionFit: Strides are long steps, so as a verb it means to walk purposefully.

clue.text: See 17
Possible place for grapevine gossip? Nice water

parts.note: chat is idle gossip
in Nice, a French city, water is eau

explanation.surface: The office grapevine, where gossip flows nicely by the water cooler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice' is the French city, not 'pleasant'; 'grapevine' means the rumour mill in the surface, real vines in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A French wine estate is a château, where grapevines are grown, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Doctor inhales lit piece (heroin and crack)

indicators.note: inhales means takes in, so the other letters go inside
lit is slang for drunk, signalling the letters reeling into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
H is drug slang for heroin

explanation.surface: A doctor who takes drugs, inhaling heroin and crack while intoxicated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like an anagram signal but is DR; 'lit' scrambles PIECE with H to give ECIPHE.
explanation.definitionFit: To crack a code is to work it out, which is what to decode or decipher means.

clue.text: Hit in the morning — money coming into question?

indicators.note: coming into means entering, so these letters go inside

parts.note: why is a question word
a.m. marks times in the morning
M is an abbreviation for money, as in M1 and M3

explanation.surface: A morning setback when money comes into question.
explanation.definitionFit: A whammy is a blow or setback, as in a double whammy, so it means a hit.

clue.text: "Reinventing the wheel" inapt: it's not needed

indicators.note: to reinvent is to remake something afresh, so the letters are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: Business cliché: reinventing the wheel is unsuitable as it's unnecessary.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of THE WHEEL INAPT runs over both lights, 22 down and 11 across.
explanation.definitionFit: A white elephant is a costly possession of no real use, something nobody needs.

clue.text: Staff love to take last of low-hanging fruit

indicators.note: to take means to accept inside, so the pick goes within the other letters

parts.note: to staff a desk is to man it
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

indicators.note: last of means the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Office staff love going for the low-hanging fruit, the easy wins.
explanation.definitionFit: The mango is a tropical stone fruit, so the answer is an example of a fruit.

clue.text: State "going forward", on the contrary, poster having a short opening

indicators.note: going forward is named only so its contrary can be meant, reading the other way
on the contrary turns the forward direction into backwards reading

parts.note: an ad, a poster advert

indicators.note: short means cutting the final letter

parts.note: a vent is an opening

explanation.surface: Jargon-heavy office speak about a poster with a brief opening going forward.
explanation.walkthrough: AD + A + VEN (VENT shortened) gives ADAVEN, read backwards because the clue says the opposite of 'going forward'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nevada is one of the fifty states of the USA, home to Las Vegas.

clue.text: "Steer" to enter these businesses? One points to ambition

indicators.note: to means the following letters are added to the end

parts.note: drive is ambition or energy
I is the Roman numeral one
N and S are compass points, north and south

explanation.surface: Steer into a business where one points the way to ambition.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: you steer your car into a drive-in cinema or restaurant.
explanation.definitionFit: Drive-ins are cinemas and diners you enter by car, steering in to be served.

clue.text: One cuts confusion, having switched first half

indicators.note: switching the first half means only the opening two letters swap round

parts.note: a daze is a state of confusion

explanation.surface: Someone who cuts through confusion by changing tack halfway.
explanation.definitionFit: An adze is a cutting tool like an axe, with its blade at right angles to the handle.

clue.text: Rolling Stones out, individually sustained in music

indicators.note: rolling stones gather no moss; here rolling means tumbling the letters into a new order

explanation.surface: The Rolling Stones playing music, each sustained individually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolling' is part of the band's name but is the anagram signal on STONES OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Sostenuto is an Italian direction telling players to hold each note for its full length.
